title: Haematinics
subtitle: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate
summary: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate
introduction: Interpret ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate with FBC indices, CRP/inflammation, renal/liver disease, diet, bleeding history and neurological symptoms.

rows.name: Ferritin
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult reference: men ≥19 y 30–400 µg/L; women 19–59 y 15–150 µg/L; women ≥60 y 15–330 µg/L
notes: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein and may be normal or raised despite iron deficiency during infection, inflammation, liver disease or malignancy.

rows.name: Transferrin saturation
notes: Low saturation with low ferritin supports absolute iron deficiency. Low saturation with normal/high ferritin may reflect inflammation, CKD or mixed deficiency.

rows.name: Vitamin B12
rows.referenceRange: RVH/NICE NG239 interpretation: <180 ng/L confirmed deficiency; 180–350 ng/L indeterminate/possible deficiency; >350 ng/L deficiency unlikely
notes: Deficiency can produce macrocytosis, glossitis, paraesthesia, impaired vibration/proprioception, gait disturbance, cognitive change or pancytopenia. Neurological deficiency can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis.

rows.name: Folate
notes: Low folate can cause macrocytic anaemia. Replace B12 deficiency first or concurrently; folate alone can improve anaemia while neurological B12 injury progresses.

urgentFindings: Anaemia with chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest, hypotension or active bleeding.
New gait disturbance, objective sensory loss, weakness, cognitive change or bladder/bowel symptoms with possible B12 deficiency.
Pancytopenia, rapidly falling haemoglobin or platelets, or haemolysis features (jaundice, dark urine, raised bilirubin/LDH).
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Absolute iron deficiency picture
findings: No active infection or inflammation to explain a falsely normal ferritin
interpretation: Low ferritin with low transferrin saturation supports true (absolute) iron deficiency, most often from chronic blood loss or poor intake/absorption
This combination is more reliable than ferritin alone, which can be falsely normal in inflammation
actions: Ask about GI bleeding, menstrual/obstetric history, diet and any malabsorptive condition
Request FBC to assess for associated microcytic anaemia (see further testing)
Arrange medical review for further investigation of the bleeding source, particularly in patients over 50 or with new symptoms

commonPatterns.title: Functional iron deficiency with inflammation
findings: Known infection, chronic inflammatory disease, liver disease or malignancy
interpretation: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein and can be normal or raised despite true iron deficiency when inflammation is present, masking the deficiency on ferritin alone
Low transferrin saturation despite a normal/high ferritin suggests iron is not being made available for erythropoiesis, either from true co-existing deficiency or from inflammation itself
actions: Correlate with CRP and the activity of the underlying inflammatory condition (see further testing)
Consider that this pattern can reflect true iron deficiency being masked by inflammation, not just anaemia of chronic disease
Arrange medical review if the distinction affects treatment (e.g. considering iron replacement) or the cause of inflammation is unclear

commonPatterns.title: Confirmed B12 deficiency
findings: Macrocytosis, glossitis, paraesthesia, gait disturbance or cognitive change may or may not be present
interpretation: Meets the threshold for confirmed deficiency; neurological B12 deficiency can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis, so a normal FBC does not exclude clinically important deficiency
New objective neurological signs (gait disturbance, sensory loss, weakness) represent a more urgent presentation than an isolated low result
actions: Examine for objective neurological signs (gait, vibration/proprioception, weakness) rather than relying on symptoms alone
Treat as time-critical if new gait disturbance, objective sensory loss, weakness, cognitive change or bladder/bowel symptoms are present (see urgent findings)
Arrange medical review for replacement and investigation of the underlying cause (e.g. pernicious anaemia, dietary, malabsorption)

commonPatterns.title: Indeterminate B12 result
interpretation: This range does not confirm or exclude deficiency; clinical correlation and, where available, further testing (e.g. active B12/MMA) or a trial of replacement guided by specialist/local pathway may be needed
Treating on symptoms alone despite an indeterminate result is a reasonable and common approach when clinical suspicion is high
actions: Correlate with symptoms, FBC/blood film and risk factors (poor diet, malabsorption, metformin use, older age)
Discuss with the requesting clinician or follow the local pathway for indeterminate results rather than dismissing symptoms
Arrange medical review if neurological or haematological features are present despite the indeterminate result

commonPatterns.title: Low folate — confirm B12 status before treating
findings: B12 status not yet known or not checked
interpretation: Folate deficiency can cause macrocytic anaemia, but replacing folate without knowing B12 status risks masking or worsening B12 deficiency — folate can improve the anaemia while B12-related neurological injury continues to progress
actions: Confirm B12 has been checked (or is being checked) before folate replacement is started
Ask about diet, alcohol use and malabsorptive conditions as causes of folate deficiency
Arrange medical review if B12 deficiency cannot be excluded, or if there are any neurological features (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Combined deficiency picture
findings: More than one of iron, B12 or folate low or borderline
RDW raised or a mixed picture on FBC indices
interpretation: Combined deficiencies are common, particularly with poor overall dietary intake, malabsorption (e.g. coeliac disease, bariatric surgery, alcohol excess) or in frail older adults, and can partially mask each other on the FBC (e.g. normal MCV despite significant deficiency)
actions: Take a broad dietary, alcohol and gastrointestinal history rather than assuming a single isolated deficiency
Request coeliac serology or consider malabsorption work-up if no clear dietary cause is found (see further testing)
Arrange medical review for coordinated replacement, since correcting one deficiency can unmask or worsen another if not addressed together

furtherTesting.test: Full blood count and blood film
rationale: Provides the red-cell indices (MCV, RDW) and morphology that support and characterise a deficiency picture identified on haematinics
Helps determine whether a normal or raised ferritin reflects true iron sufficiency or is being masked by an acute-phase response
Malabsorption from undiagnosed coeliac disease is a recognised and treatable cause of iron, B12 and/or folate deficiency, particularly when combined or unexplained
Identifies renal or hepatic disease that can contribute to anaemia and affects interpretation and safety of any replacement therapy
Helps confirm a marrow response once deficiency replacement has started, and supports assessment for haemolysis as an alternative or additional cause of macrocytic anaemia
Confirms response to replacement therapy and helps distinguish an indeterminate or borderline result from true deficiency over time

specimens.notes: Plasma — green-top lithium-heparin tube with yellow insert, 3 mL. Protect folate and vitamin B12 samples from light; fasting is preferred for vitamin B12.
